sentences.text: The name Necrosuchus combines the Greek words for 'dead' and 'crocodile', inspired by a question from a well-meaning lady.
Necrosuchus is distinguished from other caimans by having its 13th lower jaw tooth as the second largest, a trait shared only with Purussaurus brasiliensis and some Paleosuchus species.
Evidence suggests the holotype specimen of Necrosuchus died before reaching full adult size, as indicated by unfused vertebrae sutures.
Fossils of Necrosuchus were discovered on April 3, 1931, during the First Scarritt Expedition in Argentina.
The genus Necrosuchus was first described by George G. Simpson in 1937.
Detailed descriptions of the postcranial skeleton of Necrosuchus were not published until 2012.
Necrosuchus is classified within the family Alligatoridae.
Research indicates that Necrosuchus possesses derived features characteristic of alligatoroids, specifically within the subfamily Caimaninae.
A 2020 study placed Necrosuchus as a derived member of Caimaninae, though its exact position remains uncertain due to a large polytomy involving modern caimans and Purussaurus.
In phylogenetic analyses, Necrosuchus is often recovered as a parent group or close relative of the genus Jacarea.
Necrosuchus lived approximately 60 million years ago during the Paleocene epoch in what is now Argentina.
Necrosuchus inhabited marine or river-lake environments within the Patagonian Salamanca Formation.
The time range for Necrosuchus is estimated to be between 66 and 61.66 million years ago.
